patient.name: Aisha Rahman
patient.setting: GP surgery, then Emergency Department six months later
patient.complaint: Four months of night-time cough, wheeze and chest tightness
background: Eczema as a child; hay fever every summer
Lives in Walthamstow with her partner and a cat

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with episodic, variable wheeze worse at night in an atopic young person, and 'How severe is this attack?' questions that hinge on PEF %, RR, HR and A CHEST 92.

points: Aisha, 26, wakes at 4 am **coughing and wheezy** most nights.
Chest feels tight after visiting friends with **cats** and in smoky bars.
Symptoms come and go; some weeks she is completely well.
Childhood **eczema**, summer **hay fever**, mother has asthma.

steps.lead: Aisha's variable, trigger-driven symptoms fit **reversible airway obstruction** from a Type I hypersensitivity reaction.
She is **atopic** (eczema, hay fever) with a family history: the classic risk profile. Adult onset would also make you ask about her job.
**Episodic** wheeze, worse at night, with clear triggers, and she wakes several nights a week: her asthma is not controlled.
Aisha takes ibuprofen without problems and has no polyps, so she does not have **Samter's triad**, but always ask about aspirin and NSAIDs.
If Aisha later had worsening wheeze with **very high eosinophils** despite treatment, think **ABPA**, an asthma complication.

points: Six months later: Aisha arrives in ED after a weekend with a friend's cats.
She cannot finish a sentence; speaks in short phrases.
PEF **190 L/min**; her best is 450 L/min.

visual.title: Aisha's PEF (% of best)
visual.label: Aisha 42%
visual.caption: 190/450 = 42%: in the **33-50%** band. Add RR 28 and HR 118 and she has **acute severe** asthma.

steps.q: PEF 42%, RR 28, HR 118, cannot complete sentences, SpO2 93%. How severe is Aisha's attack?
steps.r: PEF 33-50%, RR 25 or more, HR 110 or more and incomplete sentences = **acute severe**. SpO2 is above 92% and she is not exhausted, so not life-threatening.

steps.lead: Grade every attack from the numbers. Aisha is **acute severe** now; any A CHEST 92 feature would make her life-threatening.

steps.text: A **quiet chest** is not improvement: a silent chest means almost no air movement and is **life-threatening**. Read the stem for exhaustion, confusion or a falling respiratory rate.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (FeNO in children, eosinophils/FeNO then spirometry with reversibility in adults; serial PEF for occupational asthma), and ABG thresholds in an acute attack.

steps.q: At the GP surgery, which first test best supports a diagnosis of asthma in Aisha?
steps.r: Markers of **eosinophilic inflammation** come first in practice; spirometry with reversibility follows if they are not diagnostic. A chest X-ray is usually normal.

steps.lead: Aisha's FeNO is **62 ppb** (above 50) and her eosinophils are raised: both point to eosinophilic asthma.

visual.title: Aisha's FeNO
visual.label: Aisha 62
visual.caption: Above **50 ppb** in an adult supports asthma. In a child aged 5-16 the cut-off is **35 ppb**.

steps.title: Spirometry with reversibility
steps.text: Obstructive pattern with **preserved FVC**, and FEV1 rises **18%** after salbutamol: reversible obstruction.

steps.lead: Aisha's FEV1 rose by more than **12%** after salbutamol, which confirms reversible obstruction.
Had spirometry been unavailable, a 2 week **PEF diary** with more than 20% variability would support her diagnosis.

points: Back to ED: after first nebulisers Aisha looks tired.
She now speaks only single words.

steps.title: ABG (on oxygen)
steps.text: Sats below 92% means an ABG. A **'normal' pCO2** in a breathless asthmatic is ominous: she is tiring.

steps.lead: Aisha's sats fell below **92%**, so she needed an ABG; it upgrades her to **life-threatening** asthma.

visual.title: Aisha's pCO2 (serial gases) and RR in ED
visual.caption: pCO2 climbing back to 'normal' while RR falls is **exhaustion**, not recovery.

steps.text: Do not treat a **pCO2 of 5.4 kPa** as reassuring in acute asthma. Hyperventilating patients should have a low pCO2; a normal or rising value means imminent respiratory failure.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the next most appropriate step?' on the NICE ladder (AIR, then MART up the doses, then FeNO/eosinophils, LTRA or LAMA, specialist) and acute steps: oxygen, nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, prednisolone, then IV magnesium.

steps.q: Aisha is newly diagnosed. Which is the most appropriate first treatment?
steps.r: First-line is a **low-dose ICS/formoterol** combination inhaler used as needed. SABA alone leaves inflammation untreated.

steps.lead: Aisha starts low-dose **budesonide/formoterol** as needed and is told to **rinse her mouth** after each use.
If she still had symptoms, the next step is **low-dose MART**: the same inhaler regularly plus as needed.

steps.title: NICE ladder
nodes: Raised: specialist; not raised: add LTRA or LAMA
steps.caption: Check adherence and inhaler technique before every step up.

steps.lead: Each review moves Aisha up or down this ladder. Once controlled for 3 months she can step down by **25-50%**.

steps.q: Aisha in ED: acute severe, SpO2 93%. Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
o: Nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium with oral prednisolone
steps.r: First-line: **oxygen-driven nebulised salbutamol** plus **ipratropium** and **prednisolone 40-50 mg**. Magnesium comes only if she fails to respond.

steps.lead: Aisha gets oxygen to keep sats **94-98%**, back-to-back nebs and prednisolone 40 mg. ITU are told when she deteriorates.
When Aisha tired with a normal pCO2, she got **IV magnesium sulphate** and an ITU review. She improved without intubation.

visual.title: Aisha's PEF (% of best) over 3 days
visual.caption: After magnesium she turns the corner. On day 3 her PEF is above **75%** off nebulisers.

steps.lead: Aisha was stable off nebulisers and oxygen for **24 hours** with PEF 81%, so she met discharge criteria.
Aisha's care followed NICE (ladder, FeNO thresholds) and BTS/SIGN (attack severity).

steps.text: Before discharge: check **inhaler technique**, give a written **asthma action plan**, a short course of prednisolone and a GP review within 2 working days. She moves up to **low-dose MART**.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanisms: mast cell degranulation in Type I hypersensitivity, why salbutamol reverses obstruction (beta-2, cAMP), why a normal pCO2 is ominous, and how magnesium relaxes smooth muscle.

steps.title: Cat dander to bronchospasm
nodes: Allergen binds IgE on mast cells
Smooth muscle contracts, mucosa swells, mucus increases
steps.caption: Type I (immediate) hypersensitivity: IgE-mediated.

steps.lead: Aisha's attack began when **cat allergen** cross-linked IgE on her mast cells.
Her raised FeNO and eosinophils reflect **Th2-driven eosinophilic** airway inflammation.
Her FEV1 rose 18% with salbutamol because the obstruction is smooth muscle spasm that **beta-2 agonism** relaxes.

steps.q: How does salbutamol relax Aisha's bronchial smooth muscle?
steps.r: Salbutamol is a **beta-2 agonist**: Gs protein, more cAMP, smooth muscle relaxation. Ipratropium blocks muscarinic receptors.

steps.lead: Regular ICS in her MART inhaler suppress cytokines and **eosinophil recruitment**, cutting future attacks.
Aisha's pCO2 rose from 3.9 to 5.4 kPa as her **respiratory muscles fatigued**.
Magnesium **blocks calcium entry** into smooth muscle cells, so they relax even when nebulisers have failed.

steps.text: Montelukast blocks **leukotriene** receptors; ICS block cytokine production. Know which mediator each drug targets.

mcq.q: What type of hypersensitivity reaction is asthma?

o: PEF 33-50%, RR 25 or more, HR 110 or more
mcq.r: PEF **33-50%**, RR **≥25**, HR **≥110** or unable to complete sentences.
Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease: asthma, **nasal polyps**, **aspirin sensitivity**.

mcq.q: What is the most common cause of occupational asthma?
mcq.r: **Isocyanates** (spray paints, foams) are the commonest cause.

mcq.q: What rise in FEV1 after a bronchodilator is diagnostic of asthma?
What FeNO level is diagnostic of asthma in a child aged 5-16?
mcq.r: **≥35 ppb** in children; above 50 ppb in adults.

mcq.q: What is the first IV treatment if an acute attack fails to respond to nebulisers and steroids?
mcq.r: **IV magnesium** first, then aminophylline, then IV salbutamol.

mcq.q: Which is a discharge criterion after an acute asthma attack?
mcq.r: PEF **>75%** and stable off nebulisers and oxygen for **12-24 hours**.

mcq.q: Why is a normal pCO2 ominous in a severe asthma attack?
o: It means the patient is tiring
mcq.r: She should be hyperventilating (low pCO2); 'normal' means **fatigue**.

mcq.q: How does magnesium sulphate relax bronchial smooth muscle?
mcq.r: Magnesium **blocks calcium influx** into smooth muscle cells.

prompts.q: What is asthma, and who gets it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: reversible obstruction in an atopic young person; adult onset means ask about work.

points.p: Chronic inflammatory airway disease with reversible obstruction (Type I hypersensitivity)
Atopy (eczema, hay fever) and family history
Often begins in childhood
Occupational asthma: isocyanates commonest

prompts.q: How does asthma present, and what shows it is poorly controlled?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: variability is the key word.

points.p: Variable, episodic wheeze, cough, breathlessness, chest tightness
Worse at night and early morning
Triggers such as cats, smoke, exercise, cold
Poor control: night waking, daytime symptoms 3 or more times a week, attack in 2 years

prompts.q: What are the features of acute severe asthma, and of life-threatening asthma (A CHEST 92)?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: always calculate the PEF %.

points.p: Moderate: PEF 50-75%
Acute severe: PEF 33-50%, RR 25 or more, HR 110 or more, cannot complete sentences
Life-threatening: PEF under 33%, SpO2 under 92%
Altered consciousness, cyanosis, hypotension, exhaustion, silent chest, bradycardia or poor effort
points.why: A silent chest is not improvement.

points.p: Near-fatal: raised pCO2 or needing ventilation

prompts.q: What is Samter's triad and what complication of asthma gives marked eosinophilia?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: polyps plus NSAIDs; eosinophils plus failed antibiotics.

points.p: Samter's triad: asthma, nasal polyps, aspirin sensitivity (AERD)
ABPA: wheeze, cough, eosinophilia, with asthma or bronchiectasis
Curschmann spirals on histology

prompts.q: Which tests diagnose asthma, with their cut-offs?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: child = FeNO first; spirometry needs 12% reversibility.

points.p: FeNO: 35 ppb or more in children 5-16, above 50 ppb in adults
Blood eosinophils above upper limit (0.4)
Spirometry with reversibility: FEV1 rises 12% or more after salbutamol
PEF diary over 2 weeks: variability above 20%
Bronchial challenge if unclear; serial PEF at work and home for occupational
points.why: Work and home diary links it to the job.

prompts.q: When is an ABG done in acute asthma, and what result is most worrying?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the number 92, and a normal pCO2.

points.p: ABG if SpO2 below 92%
A normal pCO2 (4.6-6.0 kPa) is ominous
points.why: She should be blowing it off.

points.p: Raised pCO2 = near-fatal, needs ventilation

prompts.q: What are the steps of the NICE long-term asthma ladder?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: check technique and adherence, then climb one rung.

points.p: As-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol
points.why: Rinse the mouth to prevent candidiasis.

points.p: Low-dose MART
Moderate-dose MART
Check FeNO and eosinophils: raised refer; not raised add LTRA or LAMA
Specialist referral; step down by 25-50% after 3 months' control

prompts.q: How is acute severe asthma treated, and what comes next if it fails?

points.p: Oxygen to SpO2 94-98%
Nebulised salbutamol (oxygen-driven) plus ipratropium
Prednisolone 40-50 mg oral (IV hydrocortisone 100 mg if vomiting)
IV magnesium sulphate, then IV aminophylline, then IV salbutamol
Inform ITU; intubate if treatment fails
points.why: Especially after a previous near-fatal attack.

prompts.q: What are the discharge criteria after an acute attack?

points.p: Stable on discharge medication (no nebulisers or oxygen) for 12-24 hours
PEF above 75% of best or predicted
points.why: Check technique and give an action plan.

points.p: Pregnant women with a severe attack are admitted even if improved

prompts.q: What happens in the airway in asthma, and why does spirometry reverse?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: IgE, mast cells, mediators, beta-2.

points.p: Allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells, which degranulate
Histamine and leukotrienes released
Smooth muscle contraction, mucosal oedema, mucus hypersecretion
Salbutamol: beta-2 agonist, raises cAMP, relaxes smooth muscle

prompts.q: Why do ICS, magnesium and a normal pCO2 matter mechanistically?

points.p: ICS suppress cytokines and eosinophil recruitment
Magnesium blocks calcium influx into smooth muscle
Normal pCO2 means fatigue: cannot maintain minute ventilation

glossary.Atopy: An inherited tendency to make IgE to allergens, giving asthma, eczema and hay fever.
glossary.Type I hypersensitivity: Immediate allergic reaction mediated by IgE on mast cells, occurring within minutes.
glossary.Mast cell: Tissue immune cell that releases histamine and leukotrienes when IgE on its surface is cross-linked.
glossary.Leukotrienes: Inflammatory mediators that constrict bronchi and increase mucus; blocked by montelukast.
glossary.Eosinophils: White cells that drive allergic airway inflammation; raised in eosinophilic asthma.
glossary.FeNO: Fractional exhaled nitric oxide: a breath test that measures eosinophilic airway inflammation.
glossary.ppb: Parts per billion, the unit for FeNO.
glossary.PEF: Peak expiratory flow: the fastest rate a person can blow out, in L/min.
glossary.PEFR: Peak expiratory flow rate; the same as PEF.
glossary.FEV1: Forced expiratory volume in 1 second: air blown out in the first second of a forced breath.
glossary.FVC: Forced vital capacity: total air blown out after a full breath in.
glossary.FEV1/FVC: The ratio of FEV1 to FVC; below 0.7 means airflow obstruction.
glossary.Reversibility: Improvement in FEV1 after a bronchodilator; 12% or more supports asthma.
glossary.Bronchial challenge test: Inhaling methacholine or histamine to provoke airway narrowing; shows hyperresponsiveness.
glossary.SABA: Short-acting beta-2 agonist, such as salbutamol; a reliever.
glossary.LABA: Long-acting beta-2 agonist, such as formoterol or salmeterol.
glossary.ICS: Inhaled corticosteroid, such as budesonide or beclometasone; a preventer.
glossary.Formoterol: A LABA with a fast onset, so it can be used as a reliever with ICS.
glossary.MART: Maintenance and reliever therapy: one ICS/formoterol inhaler used regularly and as needed.
glossary.LTRA: Leukotriene receptor antagonist, such as montelukast.
glossary.Montelukast: An oral leukotriene receptor antagonist used as an asthma add-on.
glossary.LAMA: Long-acting muscarinic antagonist, such as tiotropium.
glossary.Ipratropium: A short-acting muscarinic antagonist bronchodilator, nebulised in acute asthma.
glossary.Aminophylline: An IV theophylline salt used in refractory acute asthma; narrow therapeutic range.
glossary.Magnesium sulphate: IV drug that relaxes bronchial smooth muscle by blocking calcium influx.
glossary.A CHEST 92: Mnemonic for life-threatening asthma: altered consciousness, cyanosis, hypotension, exhaustion, silent chest, tachy/bradyarrhythmia, PEF <33%, SpO2 <92%.
glossary.Silent chest: Almost no breath sounds because so little air moves; a life-threatening sign.
glossary.Near-fatal asthma: Raised pCO2 or need for mechanical ventilation with raised inflation pressures.
glossary.ABG: Arterial blood gas: measures pH, oxygen and carbon dioxide in arterial blood.
glossary.pCO2: Partial pressure of carbon dioxide in blood; normal 4.7 to 6.0 kPa.
glossary.Minute ventilation: Volume of air breathed per minute: respiratory rate times tidal volume.
glossary.Samter's triad: Asthma, nasal polyps and aspirin sensitivity.
glossary.AERD: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, also called Samter's triad.
glossary.Nasal polyps: Benign grey swellings of the nasal lining causing blockage and loss of smell.
glossary.Curschmann spirals: Spiral mucus plugs from small airways seen in asthmatic sputum or histology.
glossary.ABPA: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis: allergic reaction to Aspergillus in asthma, with eosinophilia and high IgE.
glossary.Occupational asthma: Adult-onset asthma caused by a workplace agent; better away from work.
glossary.Isocyanates: Chemicals in spray paints and foams; the commonest cause of occupational asthma.
glossary.Oral candidiasis: Oral thrush, a side effect of inhaled steroids; prevented by rinsing the mouth.
glossary.Asthma action plan: Written plan telling the patient how to adjust treatment and when to seek help.
glossary.cAMP: Cyclic AMP: a second messenger that relaxes smooth muscle when raised by beta-2 agonists.
glossary.IgE: The antibody class that binds mast cells and drives allergic reactions.
glossary.Th2: T helper 2 cells, which drive allergic, eosinophilic inflammation.

technique.stem: A 19 year old man has a severe attack of asthma. He is drowsy and can only say single words. His chest is quiet on auscultation. His temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 128 bpm, BP 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% on 15 L/min oxygen. PEF is 120 L/min (best 520 L/min).
technique.q: Which is the most accurate classification of this attack?

steps.x: A severity question: calculate PEF % first, then scan for A CHEST 92.
PEF 120/520 = 23%. Altered consciousness, silent chest, sats below 92%, a falling RR: exhaustion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Any A CHEST 92 feature: **life-threatening**.

elim: PEF is under 33% and there are A CHEST 92 features, so it is worse than acute severe.
Moderate is PEF 50-75% with no severe features.
Not a BTS acute severity grade, and he is critically unwell.
Drowsiness here is from hypoxia and fatigue, not seizures.

steps.x: **B. Life-threatening asthma.** Rule: one A CHEST 92 feature makes it life-threatening; a raised pCO2 needing ventilation is near-fatal.

technique.stem: A 31 year old woman has a 6 month history of intermittent wheeze and nocturnal cough. Her blood eosinophil count and FeNO are borderline. Examination is normal between episodes. Spirometry is arranged.

steps.x: An investigation-result question: what must spirometry show to confirm this condition?
Variable symptoms, inconclusive first-line markers: spirometry with reversibility next.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: An FEV1 rise of **12% or more** after a bronchodilator is diagnostic.

elim: This is normal spirometry.
Under 12%: not significant reversibility.
A restrictive pattern (e.g. fibrosis).
Points to emphysema or interstitial disease; TLCO is normal in asthma.

steps.x: **A. FEV1 rise of 15% after salbutamol.** Rule: ≥12% FEV1 reversibility = asthma.

technique.stem: A 28 year old woman has acute severe asthma. She has received oxygen, two back-to-back nebulised salbutamol doses, nebulised ipratropium and oral prednisolone 40 mg. After 30 minutes, her PEF is 35% of best and she is still wheezy. Her pulse rate is 122 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 27 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% on oxygen.
technique.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now.
First-line treatment done, still acute severe.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The first add-on when first-line fails: **IV magnesium sulphate**.

elim: Second-line after magnesium, with senior input.
A last resort in life-threatening asthma.
A long-term add-on, not acute rescue.
For failure of all therapy or near-fatal asthma; she is not exhausted.

steps.x: **C. IV magnesium sulphate.** Order: magnesium, then aminophylline, then IV salbutamol, then ventilation.

technique.stem: A 22 year old man with asthma develops wheeze within 10 minutes of stroking a friend's cat. His blood total IgE is raised and skin prick testing to cat dander is positive.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his acute bronchoconstriction?
o: Antibody binding to airway basement membrane
Cross-linking of IgE on mast cells causing degranulation

steps.x: A science question: link the clinical picture to its mechanism.

clues: skin prick testing to cat dander is positive
steps.x: Minutes after allergen, IgE-driven: immediate hypersensitivity.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Type I: allergen cross-links IgE on **mast cells**, releasing histamine and leukotrienes.

elim: A Type II mechanism (e.g. Goodpasture's).
Type III (e.g. hypersensitivity pneumonitis acute phase).
More typical of COPD than allergic asthma.
Type IV takes 48-72 hours, not minutes.

steps.x: **C. Cross-linking of IgE on mast cells causing degranulation.** Rule: minutes + IgE = Type I mast cell degranulation.

practice.stem: A 17 year old boy has a 3 month history of cough and wheeze that wake him in the early morning. Symptoms are worse after football and around his grandmother's cat. He had eczema as a child. Between episodes his chest is clear. His pulse rate is 76 bpm, BP 118/70 mmHg and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Episodic, nocturnal wheeze with triggers in an atopic young person is asthma. COPD needs age and smoking, and is persistent.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before reading the options.

clues: wake him in the early morning
steps.x: Variable nocturnal and early morning symptoms, triggers, atopy, normal between episodes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Episodic variable wheeze in an atopic teenager: **asthma**.

elim: Daily large-volume purulent sputum, not variable wheeze.
Needs age over 35 and a smoking history; persistent, not episodic.
Can cause cough, but no wheeze with allergen or exercise triggers.
Inspiratory stridor-like noise; no atopy or nocturnal pattern.

steps.x: **A. Asthma.** Variable + nocturnal + atopy = asthma.

practice.stem: A 24 year old woman with asthma has had worsening breathlessness for 2 days. She is wheezy and cannot complete sentences. Her temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 27 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. PEF is 180 L/min (best 420 L/min).
practice.q: Which is the most accurate classification of this attack?
practice.e: PEF 43% with RR 27, HR 116 and inability to complete sentences is acute severe asthma. There are no A CHEST 92 features.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before reading the options.
PEF 180/420 = 43%. RR 27, HR 116, incomplete sentences, sats 94%.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: PEF 33-50% with RR ≥25 and HR ≥110: **acute severe**.

elim: No A CHEST 92 features: SpO2 94%, PEF over 33%, alert.
Moderate is PEF 50-75% without severe features.
Needs a raised pCO2 or need for ventilation.
She is having an acute attack.

steps.x: **A. Acute severe asthma.** Calculate the PEF % every time.

practice.stem: A 30 year old man with asthma has had nebulised salbutamol in the emergency department. He is now exhausted and confused, and his chest is silent. His pulse rate is 52 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg and oxygen saturation 88% on 15 L/min oxygen.
practice.q: Which is the most accurate classification of this attack?
practice.e: Exhaustion, confusion, silent chest, bradycardia, hypotension and sats below 92% are A CHEST 92 features: life-threatening asthma. A pCO2 above 6.0 kPa or need for ventilation would make it near-fatal.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before reading the options.
Exhaustion, altered consciousness, silent chest, bradycardia, hypotension, sats below 92%.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A CHEST 92 features: **life-threatening asthma**.

elim: He has several A CHEST 92 features, so it is worse than acute severe.
Describes a pattern of sudden attacks over time, not this attack's grade.
Moderate means PEF 50-75% with no severe features.
Describes day-to-day control, not an acute attack.

steps.x: **C. Life-threatening asthma.** A silent chest is never improvement.

practice.stem: A 45 year old woman has had asthma for 5 years and a blocked nose with loss of smell. Nasal examination shows bilateral grey, glistening masses. Within an hour of taking ibuprofen for back pain she became very wheezy.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Asthma, nasal polyps and aspirin/NSAID sensitivity form Samter's triad (AERD). Avoid NSAIDs.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before reading the options.
Asthma, nasal polyps, NSAID-triggered wheeze.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Samter's triad**: aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease.

elim: Gives productive cough, eosinophilia and bronchiectasis, not an NSAID reaction.
Eosinophilic vasculitis with neuropathy or rash; polyps alone do not make it.
Causes polyps but presents in childhood with bronchiectasis.
Linked to work exposure, not NSAIDs.

steps.x: **B. Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease.** Asthma + polyps + aspirin/NSAID sensitivity = Samter's triad.

practice.stem: A 47 year old man has had asthma since childhood. Over 6 months he has had repeated episodes of wheeze and cough productive of brown plugs, despite an inhaled corticosteroid and long-acting beta agonist. Several courses of antibiotics have not helped. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 90 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: ABPA complicates asthma: wheeze, cough with brown mucus plugs, marked eosinophilia and high IgE, unresponsive to antibiotics.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before reading the options.

clues: Several courses of antibiotics have not helped
steps.x: Known asthma, worsening despite treatment, mucus plugs, antibiotics useless, very high eosinophils and IgE.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: An asthma complication with eosinophilia: **ABPA**.

elim: No smoking history; does not cause marked eosinophilia.
No weight loss or haemoptysis; eosinophilia is not typical.
Night sweats and weight loss; no eosinophilia.
Would respond to antibiotics and give a neutrophilia.

steps.x: **A. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.** Asthma + eosinophilia + brown plugs + failed antibiotics = ABPA.

practice.stem: A 38 year old man works in a car body repair shop spraying paint. For 6 months he has had wheeze and chest tightness that are worse at the end of the working week and improve on holiday. He has never had asthma before. His pulse rate is 80 bpm, BP 126/82 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
practice.e: Adult-onset asthma that improves away from work is occupational asthma; isocyanates (spray paints) are the commonest cause.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before reading the options.

clues: car body repair shop spraying paint
worse at the end of the working week
steps.x: Adult-onset wheeze that improves away from work, in a spray painter.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Occupational asthma from **isocyanates** in spray paint.

elim: Causes pleural plaques, asbestosis and mesothelioma, not reversible wheeze.
Triggers would not follow his working week.
Causes berylliosis, a granulomatous lung disease.
Can cause occupational asthma, but spray paint points to isocyanates.

steps.x: **D. Isocyanates.** Adult-onset asthma better on holiday = occupational; isocyanates commonest.

practice.stem: An 11 year old girl has a 4 month history of cough and wheeze at night and with exercise. She has hay fever. Her chest is clear today. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation to support a diagnosis of asthma?
practice.e: In children aged 5-16, FeNO is the first-line test; 35 ppb or more supports asthma. Bronchodilator reversibility is next if FeNO is not raised.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show for this patient.
A child aged 5-16 with suspected asthma.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: First-line in children 5-16: **FeNO**, diagnostic at **≥35 ppb**.

elim: A bronchial challenge, used only if diagnosis remains unclear after other tests.
Usually normal in asthma; not diagnostic.
For cystic fibrosis; she has no failure to thrive or sputum.
Shows allergy, not asthma.

practice.stem: A 42 year old baker has 8 months of wheeze and cough that settle at weekends and on holiday. He had no breathing problems before this job. Spirometry with reversibility confirms asthma. The occupational health team wants evidence linking it to work.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Serial peak flow at work and at home
practice.e: Serial peak flow at work and at home (an in/out of work diary) links asthma to occupation. A single FeNO cannot show the pattern.

practice.stem: A 23 year old woman has acute severe asthma. She cannot complete sentences and is wheezy throughout. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 120/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. PEF is 40% of best. She is not vomiting.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Oxygen, nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, oral prednisolone
practice.e: First-line acute treatment is oxygen to 94-98%, oxygen-driven nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, and oral prednisolone 40-50 mg. IV magnesium comes next if she fails to respond.

practice.stem: A 34 year old man has asthma. He uses low-dose budesonide/formoterol as needed and still wakes with wheeze twice a week and uses his inhaler most days. His inhaler technique and adherence are good. His observations are normal and his chest is clear.
practice.q: According to NICE guidance, which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: On as-needed ICS/formoterol with poor control (good technique), NICE's next step is low-dose MART. LTRA or LAMA comes after moderate-dose MART.

steps.x: Uncontrolled on as-needed ICS/formoterol, technique and adherence checked.

steps.x: Next rung: **low-dose MART** (regular plus as-needed ICS/formoterol).

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman was admitted with acute severe asthma 3 days ago. She has been off nebulisers and oxygen for 24 hours. Her PEF is 82% of best. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.

o: Discharge with an action plan and GP review
practice.e: Discharge criteria are stability on discharge medication (no nebulisers or oxygen) for 12-24 hours and PEF above 75% of best.

practice.stem: A 20 year old man has a severe asthma attack. On arrival his respiratory rate is 34 breaths per minute and pCO2 is 3.6 kPa. Two hours later he is drowsy, his respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation is 90% on oxygen. His pulse rate is 130 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the change in his pCO2?
o: Respiratory muscle fatigue with falling minute ventilation
practice.e: He was hyperventilating (low pCO2). A pCO2 back to 'normal' with a falling RR and drowsiness means respiratory muscle fatigue: life-threatening asthma.

pCO2 rose to normal while RR fell and he became drowsy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: He is tiring: **respiratory muscle fatigue** reduces minute ventilation, so CO2 rises.

elim: He is drowsy with sats 90%; he is getting worse.

steps.x: **D. Respiratory muscle fatigue with falling minute ventilation.** Normal or rising pCO2 in acute asthma = exhaustion: call ITU.
